hi !
in our playgroup i'm not considered as a poor player, i think i won the
respect of others very early, but i noticed other people try to avoid to
play with me (we are often more than 20 players so it is an easy task).
Every one, even friends, fear that i'll try to break their strategy. i know
this is only a game but when you know someone, predator or prey, has a
winning strategy, why not screw him when you have the opportunity ? it may
sound no "fun" at all, but if you know someone, by doing something
insignificant right now, will certainly screw you in two or three turns, why
not screw him first ? to have the pleasure of watching his deck cycling and
applause when the combo shows up ?

yesterday, early in the game, my predator influences out Tatiana romanov
(toreador prince, +1 bleed). I influenced out the !Tremere Priscus on my
turn. When his turn came, my predator played minin tap on Tatiana, gaining 5
Pool. then he tried to 5th tradition. Everyone know what it means, because
we knew what type of deck he was playing : the super boring Minion Tap+ 5th
trad + Anson, mixed with Toreador Grand Ball, Camarila segregation and a lot
of Aching beauty and Change of target. So, when he tried to 5th tradition, i
just stopped him. At this point, he could have played a change of target but
didn't. so when we entered combat, I played Weather control, thoughts
betrayed, press, then amaranth. At this point, he lost a vampire that only
costed him 2 pool. I don't think this action negated all his chances, he
only had a slower start. Playing a Toreador deck (you know, the guys with an
small Eye on all the cards), he wasn't able to block his own predator's Jost
for all the game. He suicided himself by stacking Aching beauty on his
anson, and i never blocked him, only reduced his bleed. A lot of my dominate
bleeds were bounced at him, and everytime he put the blame on me. but why
was he unable to stop or bounce the bleed anyway ? when he was ousted, the
only thing he and my prey said was "why did you burned his vampire in the
first place ? it's your fault. "

so, i admit didn't wanted to face a predator with 40 Pool and IC & Justicars
monsters out with multiple Aching beauty on them. and i think i was right
because i won this game after all.

Is it unsportsmanship to try to avoid greater danger by removing small
threats immediatly ? Why everyone moans when i intercept their 5th tradition
anyway ?

tell me if i'm a dull, reverse play king maker, or if i was right, because
everyone here thinks i suck.

if you are also hated by other players, please tell me your story.

reyda

Messages.Author: michael...@ramstein.af.mil
Messages.Body:
Actually no, you did nothing wrong in recognizing a deck type and
stopping/delaying a key component of that deck from working properly. Some
decks have several "links" to be truly effective and if any one of those
links are severed then the deck falls apart until the link can be
reestablished.

What your predator did (from what you have written) tried to overcome a bad
starting situation and never really recovered. I know that being in a
position like that is never fun, but it does happen in the game. I can
relate to your predator as I was slammed by Legbiter in the final of a
tournament last year with his Temptation of the Greater Power deck. I never
owned a minion in the entire game for more than 1 turn without losing it. I
then ended up as a road block between my prey's intercept capability and
Legbiter's deck. I eventually took myself out just to be off the table as I
wasn't able to do anything anyway (not enough pool and large minions).

As for having people not wanting to sit next to you, I can absolutely relate.
Peter Bakija recently posted a really good article for people wanting to
start getting the hang of playing combat decks. I have been conducting this
type of play style for a long time and earned a nickname as people found out
sitting behind me was more dangerous than sitting in front of me. This
didn't mean I didn't bleed my prey, but it did mean that I did target key
minions belonging to my predator and/or grand predator (in some cases) to
slow their forward momentum and give me the time to accomplish my goal of
ousting my prey and carrying on forward.

Though I have tempered this play strategy down since coming to Europe, I still
consider it an essential part of play based upon the deck I am playing. I
have also seen this style of play a lot in the UK. I think it follows the
thought pattern of covering one's bases before you head off on the offensive.
Rob Treasure, Legbiter, Matt Green and others have provided very practical
lessons on how work this play style down to a refined art. They also have
some of the most infuriating decks I have had the pleasure to play against in
one location. Rob Treasure is in IMO probably one of the best deck
recognition players around. As to how long it takes him to make an
evaluation of the what each player is playing and develop an order of battle
to help him is something only he can answer.

If the people in your group are upset due to your growth in deck recognition
then I would suggest they need to realize that if you play the same of thing
over and over and over again, then someone somewhere is going to stop it cold
and give you a miserable time some evening. The only way they can overcome
this is to make something completely different and broaden their play with
decks they normally don't play.

Example: I use to absolutely hate political decks because of their capability
to screw the table in some manner or another. The result of this was my
occasional smacking down of one of their minions into torpor to try and keep
them in check. Since that time I have started playing Political decks to
help myself gain a better understanding of the decks (strengths and
weaknesses) So now whenever I face one on the table I have a better grasp of
what must be down to counter some or all of the deck's capabilities and what
to watch out for with trying to counter.

Try not to worry about it. If anything, you may be the catalyst within your
group that will cause other players to vary their decks and play styles.

Michael Eichler
Prince of Ramstein

That sounds like the correct answer to me. How would your predator and prey
have answered the question?

> Is it unsportsmanship to try to avoid greater danger by removing small
> threats immediatly ?

I wouldn't call Tatiana Romanov a "small threat". However, no, it is not
unsporting to do things that damage your predator and prey - not even if you're
wildly successful. In some instances, if you leave your predator too wide open
to his or her predator, it may be a mistake. But it's not unsporting.

> Why everyone moans when i intercept their 5th tradition anyway ?

Because they want their 5th tradition to be successful and they perceive that
moaning about it will result in you're doing it less often in the future -
somehow. That was not a hard question.

> tell me if i'm a dull, reverse play king maker, or if i was right, because
> everyone here thinks i suck.

Nope. I've seen this before from time to time. Sometimes predators or prey
get so frustrated about how effective one of their two main opponents is doing
against them that they forget hopes of winning and just go berserk against that
player. For that matter, most multiplayer games have elements of different
people seeing different tactics and even strategy as being "wrong" in some way
and get into kind of immature reactions about it. Myself, I get frustrated by
total "wall" reaction decks that allow one's predator to do absolutely nothing,
no matter how their deck is built, and frequently let their prey have free rein.
Or at least let their prey have free rein if he's doing directed actions against
their grandprey. Usually, that kind of deck is its own eventual punishment as
the prey often proceeds to sweep the table. I don't have to do anything.

If I were you, I'd keep on intercepting those 5th Traditions. If you have the
chance to burn your predator's minions, ask your grandpredator in front of the
whole table whether you should or not - make the discussion very open. Then, if
your predator and prey want to claim that it's not a good idea to do it, they
can argue with your grandpredator, too - not just you. If the whole table tells
you not to do it, yield to diplomacy even if you're pretty sure your right.
Sometimes, you have to play within a very silly metagame and learn its particular
rules and means for winning. Usually, if the group applies the same rules to
other players as they do to you, you can find an easier way to win the game.

Fred

Messages.Author: wes
Messages.Body:
I've recently found some of the new players in our local game are ganging up
on me (though oddly not the other veteran)...

They seem to think this is a rational way to deal not with any specific deck
of mine, but to neutralize my decks in general. While I am flattered by the
attention, I do find it makes the game lop-sided. I do not win an inordinate
amount of games (well... not with the present metagame dynamic) so I am not
sure if this is really a valid tactic or not. It is all quite freindly, mind
you, and I am not being a sore loser by mentioning this. I do however think
that this situation is similar in some ways to what Reyda is experiencing.

The strangest thing is that I am often NOT the one that is the biggest
threat in any given game. The other Jyhad-veteran (who I am sure is quite
happy to see all the attention focused on me) uses this time to set up for a
gradual sweep of the table. This has happened in enough recent games that it
is starting to concern me. Vampires will rush my vampires when there are
other targets that are obviously of more tactical benefit to the attacking
Methuselah. Bleeds will be deflected to me regardless of my position at the
table or my amount of pool. Votes will be used to damage me or affect my
minions even from across the table.

I can't seem to make clear to these players that the object of the game is
to oust you prey(s) and ultimately gain the most victory points. The object
of the game is not 'Gang up on Wes'. If I mention this, I invariably seem
like a whiner.

Generally, I really like the predator-prey dynamic of Jyhad. Sure it does
make sense to occasonally turn around and hurt your predator, but that does
not change the predator-prey relationship so much as it gives the prey a
chance to defend against a strong predator. In my local game, the
predator-prey dynamic may as well not exist.

Ironically, I think a way to try to halt this process may be to keep track
of VPs in a more formal way. If all the players can look at a sheet and say
'Gee... Wes isn't as much of a threat as we thought. Maybe we should focus
on the other guy (or try to win for ourselves)'.

Of course, another unavoidable factor in these local games is that I own
more cards than all of them combined. I have been giving away a LOT of my
cards to the new players so they will have more to work with. Mostly
vampires, commons and uncommons of course but I think it is helping. I'll
give them cards (and advice) based on what kind of deck they are trying to
build.

Any other suggestions would be greatly appreciated.

Cheers,
WES

So, whine! What's wrong? You too proud to win by begging other players
to leave you alone? Napoleon had that problem. He wound up sheep herding
in the South Atlantic.

It's a multiplayer game. If anyone does anything that damages your table
position, make sure the whole table hears you yell, "OUCH!" Mumble about
how you might as well give in now...or maybe you'll wait a turn or two before
transferring yourself out. Some of the best multiplayer gamers I know live by
creative whining. Also, creative discord-sowing, creative confusion-spreading,
and creative guilt-inducement. If you can make them dread the self-pity that
will inevitably follow each assault, the assaults will thin out. It's like
free power! Use it!

Don't just sit there and take it like a man. Bow down and grovel!
"Never whine." is a great principle for life. It sucks for playing
diplomacy-oriented games.

Fred

occasionally be stomped just so they don't sweep the table at their leisure.

someone out of the finals, or to keep yourself in... though I don't think
I'd consider that route myself.

dynamic of each particular game and bringing a particularly effective rush
deck (Please correct me if I am wrong). From the sound of it, there wasn't
really sufficient evidence that the strategy (as he detailed it) works,
though it may indeed be viable.

Collusion is a difficult thing to approach in Jyhad. I think a certain
amount of collusion is what makes this game interesting. The 'Machiavellian'
nature of the deal-making is appealing to me. What does not appeal to me is
collusion that comes from one player intending to lose but doing his/her
best to make it harder for others to win.

When a player who finds himself in a losing position suddenly decides that
instead of trying their best to win they will try to bugger up their
predator to make it harder for them to win... that's when collusion in this
game becomes ugly. It starts to become a game of revenge and doesn't
particularly appeal to me. Attacking your predator for defensive reasons
however is perfectly viable... hard to make that distinction sometimes.

similar to resigning a game of chess.

>attack-to-the-left mechanic is destroyed. An overtly strong deck is a

Nothing particular about the game in question, but 'attack to the left' is not an
absolute. If an 'upstream' deck can roll the table 'uphill', they get 2 vp, and may tie
with someone, or win by a 2-1-1(-1) count. I've been toying around with this idea; the
difficulty is in making sure your grandprey gets your grandpredator's VP in a 5-player
game.
Also note these effective uses of cross-table or backwards actions:
-- to keep those VPs available for your impending sweep.
-- to slow down/disable a predator, giving you room to move forward.
-- to forego a VP (by giving it to someone else), in order to get more VP.
-- for combat decks, to fill up an otherwise empty vamp ("I won't put him in
torpor, I just want to fill up a bit. Thanks.").

That third item leads to the point of the discussion, which deals with table mechanic. I
call it 'table skill,' ('strength' is already confusing :-) which I define as the average
skill level of the table. Basically, If I average the respective deck capabilities, play
capabilities, and game objectives over the players at a given table, group, or tournament,
I can generate a hazy bar, of which an individual player can be above (strong) or below
(weak). Overly weak or strong players at the table tend to wear a big bullseye on their
heads, as they tend to disrupt table balance.

Oh, Andrew. If Tom has, in fact, "perfected" this upstreaming tactic, I still

highly questionable in any case), he is never going to get more than 2VPs. Only

opponent more VPs than you...), thereby giving them a better chance to get into
the finals, and better seating when they are inthe finals.

As usual Andrew draws inappropriate conclusions from too little data.
For the sake of argument, I'll restate my "upstreaming tactics". When

avoid him bleeding me seriously or bouncing bleeds to me. "As often
as required" may be as seldom as not at all if a table splitting deal
can be struck with the predator. A rush deck seems to be in a
particularly strong position in offering such deals. Note that such a
deal offers me the chance at three VP and my colleague just two.

occur. In this case, "as often as required" means until all the
dangerous minions are in torpor. The time available to attend to the
prey depends on the interval between this state and the predator being
ousted. Hopefully this is long enough to make some serious progress
towards ousting him. In any case, if a new predator should appear he
must be neutralized. The pure attack to the right all the game
concept is only the fallback option if the predators should be ousted
in quick succession. Theoretically it's still possible to win in this
circumstance so it's not a disaster, but it's far from the intended
goal.

That is a very common way to play the Rush deck--table splittng deals are often
key to getting anywhere with the Rush deck. Either making a deal with your prey
(if he is another Rush deck, or if you feel if taking him out will cost you too
much) to split 3/2 with him (you getting the 2 when he rolls over for you after
getting the three), or making the oposite deal with your predator, for the 2/3
split. Either is very common, and a good way to go, especially as the Rush deck
is perfectly capable of carrying off the threat of "Well, we can fight and
*both* lose, or we can work together, and split the table..."

And again, this has nothing to do with working backwards and nullifying the
attack to the left paradigm. Oh, that Andrew.

>>At the final (or a friendly one-off game), such deals can't really
occur. In this case, "as often as required" means until all the
dangerous minions are in torpor.>>

In my book, my predator is pretty much always beaten into uselessness, but then
so is my prey. I'll ocasionally leave my predator with a minion, and even allow
him to bleed me occasionally, but if he looks at all threatening, he goes under
again.

>>The time available to attend to the prey depends on the interval between this
state and the predator being ousted.>>

I'm often a big fan of, after crippling my predator, doing everything it is
feasable (without hurting myself) to keep my crippled predator alive--helping
him with pool gaining votes, beating up his predator if things are going well
for me, etc. He usually appreciates the ability to stay in the game (if even as
a toady to his prey), and I like the safety cushion.

>>The pure attack to the right all the game concept is only the fallback option
if the predators should be ousted in quick succession. Theoretically it's
still possible to win in this circumstance so it's not a disaster, but it's far
from the intended
goal.>>

There are only a few circumstances where I'll work only to the right, and most
of them revolve around being the predator of another good Rush deck--if we
fight, we both lose the game, so I usually try to set up the 3 (for my prey)/2
(for me) VP split.

>>As I said above, I much prefer to deal than attack in preliminary
games. In the tournaments that I've attended (and many of the reports
that I've seen), numbers ranged around 18-20. With a field this size,
two VP per game pretty well assures a place at the final. At the much
larger continental tournaments, one might need to sweep at least once
to qualify.>>

6VPs is usually enough to secure the finals in most 3 preliminary rounds
tournaments, but not enough to secure a good seat. Sadly, they guy going in
with the most points gets the best seat, and so usually wins, but not always.

>>A pretty poor chance I would say. My predator should be out long
before my prey can reach him.>>

Depends on your initial prey--often just being left alone enables a quick deck
to sweep quickly. If you leave your prey alone, he ousts his prey quickly, and
moves on to your grand predator. It isn't too unlikely that the VPs end up
2/2/1, sure, but if your prey is a solid, quick deck, he can get 3 without too
much difficulty.

>>If he did get 3 VP, though, before the game reduced to the two of us, I'd be
amazed if he didn't end with 5. 18 pool is a large addition for anyone and this
guy just demonstrated that he can oust people quickly.>>

But if all of his vampires are dead, he can't hurt you :-)

>>I disagree with "reliably" and the tactic isn't meant for preliminary
rounds in any case.>>

I'd say that it is more likely that the table is split (when you work
completely to the right) 2/2/1, but a 3/2 isn't impossible.

>>As people who scored more VP than me are likely to seat as far from me as
possible, a prey on fewer VP seems a likely circumstance.>>

You'd think so, but you'd be surprised what people do. In my last tourney, the
leader in to the finals specifically chose to sit right next to my Rush deck,
because A) I played with him before and we both knew what our decks could do
and B) he knew I was willing to make deals, and stick to them. As a result of
putting himself where he was, he won.

>>All the above assumes, of course, that no one is playing any of the
several combat decks that consistently trump mine.>>

That is always the case. Every once and a while, you sit down next to Rock (a
Ventrue Obediance deck, a Gangrel Fortitude/Aggro deck) and are just screwed.
But when you don't you can do very well.

I realize that this is a Jyhad newsgroup, but I'm curious what games other
people here consider to be worth playing.

My friend and I got a bunch of old Shadowfist cards because we kept hearing
people raving about them and there were boxes going CHEAP, but it didn't
seem that great. Way too unbalanced and as you say, ganging up on the
leader.

Surprisingly, Mage knight has been a big hit around here. Personally I love
it. You can tell the guy that invented it was a fan of Chess (and CCG's for
sure). The rules are easy to learn but the strategies are deep and
compelling. I think there may be a slight balance problem, but nothing that
can't be overcome.

How is B5? I have to admit that MOST of the time I am very cautious when
looking at a game that is based on a popular franchise. In Jyhad's case,
this was less of an issue because the franchise was itself a game, so the
shoe fit quite well I think.

Since CCG's started coming out I have experimented with quite a few of them,
often buying a starter just to see if there were any interesting mechanics
to them. Some, like Battletech or Dune, have some great ideas that are
poorly implemented.

The original, Magic: the Gathering, I can respect for starting the genre,
but generally I find it too derivative and frankly, a lot of the people that
play it are... not people I want to play with. I've had more enjoyment
playing the computer version of it which goes quicker and doesn't whine when
it loses.

Jyhad always keeps me coming back, with its exceptional balance (the
three-pronged table heh), deep strategies, Machiavellian deals and the
vampire theme which originally sold me on it.

Cheers,

up holding that only copy of Enhanced Senses for turns and turns, waiting

rush action and you can't use the card anyway.

bleed for 3 or waste a vampire.

come to think of it. But my cheesy combo takes up so much room i can't pack
effective combat outside the cheesy combo, which is on my turn only.

Bah. I should try that dom/pot/cel TB pitch deck again.
